c91e725214f39495cc50576b0f9e7802195424ac.summary: A code-hosting page for a file in a public Python repository. The page lists folders (Amadey, Stealc, warzonerat) and files, including a notebook for extracting configuration from the WarzoneRAT malware family and a YARA rule file. It shows commit and archive metadata. It describes no actors, victims, campaigns or findings, so it is not a threat report.

c9af65927e7b013cfdb566cd32de2941c915ee0e.summary: eSentire's Threat Response Unit reports an opportunistic June 2021 malspam campaign by the FIN7 group, using a fake legal complaint about Brown-Forman. A law firm was a victim. The Excel lure installs the JSSLoader RAT via WMI. The report also covers FIN7's shifting lures, timed infrastructure registration, and suspected ties to Ryuk and REvil, which remain unconfirmed.

hedges: The role of one intermediate server is unclear; it may test whether a visitor is a susceptible victim rather than a security researcher.
The months-long gap before a landing page was used might have been meant to thwart reputation filters that use domain age.
The report calls the timing relative to the Brown-Forman claim deadline coincidental and says whether FIN7 is connected to the REvil attack remains to be seen.
Truesec theorized FIN7 may have sold access to the Ryuk group or may be closely affiliated with it; the report says either theory implies few sectors are out of scope.
A Swiss security company promised evidence linking FIN7 and REvil but never provided sufficient evidence, according to the report.
The report sees no apparent relationship between this infrastructure and infrastructure reported by previous research.
In-the-wild use of a newly registered lookalike domain has not been observed; the report assesses it will replace the prior one.
The report describes FIN7 selling initial access to ransomware groups as plausible, not confirmed.

c945838562918fd400a627b708e888d0b4c838d8.summary: CrowdStrike's February 2021 report (part 1 of two) describes SPRITE SPIDER and CARBON SPIDER, which from the second half of 2020 deployed Linux versions of Defray777 and Darkside ransomware against VMware ESXi hosts. The report calls this Hypervisor Jackpotting: encrypting a few hosts multiplies the affected virtual machines and pressures victims to pay. Access came through valid vCenter credentials. The report suggests that if these attacks keep succeeding, more adversaries are likely to target virtualization infrastructure.

hedges: This likely reflects the overwhelming dominance of the Windows operating system in businesses and large organizations.
It is likely CARBON SPIDER pivoted to BGH in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, which dramatically reduced in-person retail sales and hospitality business.
Compared to other BGH actors, SPRITE SPIDER was relatively late to adopt this tactic, possibly due to a desire to avoid attention.
In August 2020, the adversary began deploying Darkside, likely in order to avoid sharing profits from BGH campaigns with PINCHY SPIDER, the REvil vendor.
SPRITE SPIDER and CARBON SPIDER likely intend to impose greater harm on victims than could be achieved by their respective Windows ransomware families alone.
If these ransomware attacks on ESXi servers continue to be successful, it is likely that more adversaries will begin to target virtualization infrastructure in the medium term.
SPRITE SPIDER may delete the Defray777 binary after execution.

c9fbf6cbb9f5ab705b5081e1684ca27d4b60fa30.summary: BleepingComputer reports a wave of ransomware attacks on VMware ESXi servers that exploit CVE-2021-21974, a heap overflow in the OpenSLP service patched in February 2021. The new ESXiArgs ransomware encrypts VM files and replaces the login message and ESXi home page with ransom notes. About 120 servers were encrypted on the first day and 2,400 were detected as compromised. OVHcloud's early link to the Nevada ransomware operation was later withdrawn. Only four ransom payments were tracked, and a free recovery guide helped many victims.
